title: Isaiah (Part 2)
hook: There's a Hebrew word hiding in plain sight throughout these chapters—massa, "burden"—and it means exactly what it sounds like: something lifted and carried, borne on the back before it can be set down as speech. Isaiah doesn't just announce judgment against Babylon and the nations; he labors under it, the way a prophet must labor under any truth too heavy to hold silently. And yet the same voice that groans under the weight of Babylon's fall breaks, just chapters later, into pure doxology—"O Lord, thou art my God; I will exalt thee"—because the prophet who has seen the earth laid waste in chapter 24 somehow trusts God's "counsels of old" enough to sing in chapter 25. That whiplash between devastation and praise isn't inconsistency; it's the whole architecture of hope, built by someone who has stared long enough into darkness to know exactly how much light it takes to answer it. If you've ever carried something you couldn't yet put into words, Isaiah's burden may feel strangely familiar—come and see what he does with the weight.
